claims.evidence: http/flows/changeCarrier.json; http/exchanges/shipments.jsonl
observed: Shipment SID0009108, carrier SONOCO, status R (Ready). Three different carriers were attempted — 0000, 001, 005 — the last two with ignore_sdd, ignore_cartyp and ignore_shp_def_flg all set. Every call: HTTP 200, async COMPLETE, errorCode null, errorMessage null, resultId SID0009108. The carrier read back as SONOCO every time.
Nine watched fields were compared before and after; none moved. Nothing was damaged, because nothing happened.

The reason is NOT established. The carrier may be host-controlled on this instance, the shipment may be past the point where a carrier can change, or those carrier codes may not be valid for this lane. What is established is that the API reports success either way.
claims.consequence: This is stronger than the earlier finding that a 200 body says nothing. The async resource — the mechanism the app itself uses to detect failures, and the one that correctly reported errorCode 90011 for the hold release — also reports COMPLETE here. For this verb, the ONLY way to know whether a write worked is to read the field back and compare.
claims.method_note: The first run concluded "no change" after reading four seconds behind a POST that returned complete:false, which could not distinguish a no-op from a read that raced the async. The tool now follows the asynchronousResources_uri from the response to completion before reading. That URI must be taken from the response and not constructed: the group lives at /wm/shipments/async/{id}/resources with no verb in the path, while the hold route puts the verb in — a constructed path 404s.

claims.claim: POST /wm/locations/massupdate silently ignores a field name that is not in the screen's own mass-update field set, returning 200/COMPLETE with no error and no effect. This looked identical to the changeCarrier no-op but the cause was different: an invalid field, not a business rule.
claims.evidence: http/flows/locationMassUpdate.json
observed: First attempt targeted updateNote (a real column on the location record) with a filter scoped to storageLocation EQ COPROB01. Response 200/202, async COMPLETE, errorCode null — and the field never changed.

Driving the real UI wizard (Actions > Mass Update > filter to COPROB01 > Update Attributes) showed the true field set: movementZoneId, locationUsable, pickable, pickZoneId, summarizePicksFlag, storable, storageZoneId, position, locationTypeId, areaCode, slotId, verificationCode, velocity. updateNote is not among them.
The SAME filter, resent with field "position" instead, changed the value and a separate read confirmed it. The query filter was correct on the first attempt; only the field was wrong.

Async settlement for this route took 30-90 seconds in practice, once well past a 30s poll window — far longer than holds (~5s), waves (~5s) or carrier (~10s). A capture that gives up polling early will misdiagnose a slow success as a no-op.
claims.consequence: Two silent no-ops now share the same observable signature (200, async COMPLETE, no error, no effect) with two different causes: changeCarrier is refused by a business rule not visible in any field, this one is an invalid field name not visible without opening the real UI form. Neither is distinguishable from the API response alone. A field list for a mass-update screen must come from driving Update Attributes, never assumed from the record's own field names.
claims.method_note: Multiple test writes queued during discovery landed out of order over more than a minute, so the target briefly showed a stale intermediate value before settling. Restoration was only trusted once two consecutive reads agreed AND the specific async group's own resource confirmed COMPLETE.

claims.claim: "Cancel Work" (PUT wm/work/cancelDirectedWorks/batch) does not remove or mark the record cancelled. It moves an ACK (assigned) work request back to PEND. On a record already at PEND it is a true no-op, because there is nothing to un-assign.
claims.evidence: http/flows/cancelWork.json
observed: Work 5490414, status PEND: PUT returned 200 with an empty body, and five separate reads over 12s showed workRequestStatus unchanged at PEND.
Work 5490623, status ACK: the identical call returned 200 with an empty body, and a separate read showed workRequestStatus now PEND.
No CNCL, CANCELLED, or similar terminal status exists in either observation. The verb name promises deletion; the mechanism is un-assignment.
claims.consequence: This is a THIRD distinct cause behind the same silent-success signature seen today: changeCarrier was a business-rule refusal, locations/massupdate/updateNote was an invalid field, and this is a request that already matches the target state. All three return 200 with no error and no visible difference in the response. The verb's NAME cannot be trusted to predict its effect — "Cancel" here is closer to "release assignment" than to "delete".

claims.claim: PUT wm/waves/unallocateWave/async takes jsonData as a single record object, not an array. Every other operational write captured today (work, picks-adjacent, locations, carrier, hold) wraps its payload in an array even for one record.
claims.evidence: http/flows referenced from claims; verified against wave CSTEST2
observed: Test wave CSTEST2, status ALOC (allocated). PUT with jsonData = the whole 80-field record (bare object) returned 200 and an async receipt. The async group settled COMPLETE, errorCode null, and a separate read showed waveStatus PLAN.
Source (WM.Common.min unallocateWave): e=a.getData(); Ext.Ajax.request({jsonData:e}) — no array wrapper anywhere in the call.
claims.consequence: A caller that always wraps operational write payloads in an array — a reasonable inference from every other verb recorded today — will send the wrong shape here. Payload shape must be read per-verb from the bundle, never assumed from a pattern seen on other verbs.

claims.claim: Every one of the 15 strong verb-to-route matches from index/verb-routes.json was called once with an impossible identifier. All 15 routes exist: none returned ROUTE-MISSING (404 with a Not Found body) and none returned the empty-body CSRF-rejection 404.
claims.evidence: index/verb-route-probes.json
observed: Responses split three ways: 400 bad-request (Cancel Order, Delete Order, Unallocate Wave, Cancel Wave, Adjust Inventory, Change Replenishment Priority, Cancel Replenishment, Cancel Cross Dock), 422 unprocessable (Cancel Picks, Confirm Picks, Release Picks, Relabel LPN), and 200 accepted-without-rejecting-the-impossible-id (Cancel Work, Reset Picks, Change Wave Priority).

The 200s on an impossible id are themselves informative: a route that accepts a request naming a record that cannot exist, with no visible rejection, is a candidate for the same class of silent no-op found today on changeCarrier and locations/massupdate.
claims.consequence: The verb-to-route hypothesis generation method (handler-name matching from mined bundle routes) is now validated at the existence level for all 15 strong matches, on top of the 5 confirmed by a real round trip or observed effect (Suspend/Resume Work, Mass Update, Relabel LPN, Unallocate Wave, Cancel Work-on-ACK) and 1 confirmed refused (Change Carrier). The remaining verbs (Cancel Order, Delete Order, Cancel Picks, Confirm Picks, Release Picks, Cancel Wave, Adjust Inventory, Change Replenishment Priority, Cancel Replenishment, Cancel Cross Dock) have a real route but no real-record test: order/replenishment/pick records available on this instance carry no test marker (unlike waves CSTEST/SPTEST prefixes), so testing them was deliberately not attempted without a clearly disposable target.

claims.claim: GET /wm/work SILENTLY IGNORES a query filter on workRequestId: it returns the full unfiltered result set, with the same row count and the same first row, even when the filter names an impossible id.
claims.evidence: Filtering for 5490624, 5490566 and 999999999 each returned n=85 with first row workRequestId 5490663.
observed: A before/after check written as a filtered read therefore reports SOME OTHER ROW as if it were the target — it silently reads the wrong record and can report "no change" for a write that worked, or "changed" for one that did not.
The single-record read GET /wm/work/{id} is honoured and returns the right row (5490624 -> ACK while the filtered read claimed PEND).
This is the read-side twin of the three-vocabulary problem already recorded: workRequestId is a payload key and a response field, but not a valid filter column on this resource.

claims.claim: GET /wm/waves/{waveNumber}/picks succeeds only with NO query parameters at all. Adding the site parameters every other read on this API takes (siteId, subsites) makes it fail 500 with "Argument [warehouseId] has an unexpected number of values".
claims.evidence: Bare /wm/waves/SPTEST10/picks -> 200 with 30 rows. The same path with ?siteId=SG&subsites=---- -> 500, and with ?siteId=SG&warehouseId=SG -> 500 as well.
observed: subsites=---- expands to a warehouse list server-side, so the sub-resource — which already scopes itself by the parent wave's warehouse — sees two values for one argument.
A sweep that appends the standard site params to every URL will read zero pick rows and conclude the sub-resource is empty or dead.

claims.claim: pickIdentifier on /wm/waves/{n}/picks is a position within the returned list, not a stable key. Removing one pick renumbers the rest.
claims.evidence: Before Cancel Picks, pickIdentifier 27 carried workRequestId 5490592. After, pickIdentifier 27 carried 5490591 and every later row had shifted by one.
observed: Any artifact or retry that stores a pickIdentifier and re-reads it later addresses a DIFFERENT pick. Identify a pick by workRequestId, or by outboundOrderNumber + outboundOrderLine.
A read-act-verify cycle is only safe when the read and the write happen in the same pass, before anything can shift the list.

claims.claim: PUT /wm/work/cancelPicks/batch/async, sent the whole pick record, cancels the allocated pick: its work request disappears from the system and the demand comes back as an unallocated pick row (pickStatus P, workRequestId null) against the same order line.
claims.evidence: Wave SPTEST10, pick with workRequestId 5490595 (order 2096557290 line 0005, source EH337, qty 80). After the call, 5490595 is absent from the wave and a new pickStatus=P row for order 2096557290 line 0005 appears with source EM237. Wave pick count stayed 30.
observed: Response was 202 (not the 200 most writes here return) with an async group of type CANCELPICK; the group settled COMPLETE with errorCode null and resultId null.
Cancel Picks is therefore NOT deletion of the demand — it is de-allocation, the same shape as Cancel Work (ACK -> PEND) rather than a destructive removal.

claims.claim: POST /wm/picks/confirm/async reaches the domain layer and refuses with a real business error when the pick carries no LPN: async status FAILURE, errorCode 10845, "Invalid LPN".
claims.evidence: Wave SPTEST10 pick with workRequestId 5490593 (lpn null) -> 202, async group CONFIRMPICK, settled FAILURE 10845 "Invalid LPN", resultId "W0000011IPA8|null|null".
observed: This is the FIRST of these verbs to answer with a named business error rather than a silent no-op, so route and payload shape are both confirmed correct.

The async resources URI came back as /wm/picks/confirm/batch/async/{id}/resources — a DIFFERENT path from the /wm/picks/confirm/async that was posted to. Polling a constructed URI would have missed the failure entirely.

claims.claim: PUT /wm/picks/releasePicks/batch/async against a pick already in pickStatus R returns 202, settles COMPLETE with errorCode null, and changes nothing.
claims.evidence: Wave SPTEST10, workRequestId 5490594: pickStatus R before and after; resultId "SPTEST10|W0000011IPA9|2096557290|32|R".
observed: The resultId names the exact pick, so the call DID address the right record — this is the already-in-target-state flavour of the success-shaped-nothing pattern, not a misaddressed write.
Fourth distinct cause now recorded for the identical 200/202 + COMPLETE + errorCode null signature.
FOLLOW-UP 2026-08-19: Release Picks DOES have an observable effect — on a pick in P it moves to R. The original test used a pick already in R, so the no-op was the input, not the route.

claims.claim: PUT /wm/picking/replenishments/changePriority changes a live replenishment's priority and back. The body is a BARE object (not an array), and the value lands in the priority field even though the payload key is effectivePriority.
claims.evidence: workRequestNumber 5490429: priority 3 -> 7 -> 3, each call 200 with an EMPTY response body, read back from /wm/picking/replenishments/pendingReplenishments.
observed: Second verb found to take a bare object rather than the array every other verb here uses (the first was waves/unallocateWave).
effectivePriority stayed null throughout — the payload key and the field it writes are different names, another instance of the three-vocabulary problem.
The 200 carries no body at all, so the only proof of effect is the read-back.

claims.claim: A write can 404 with errorCode -1403 and userMessage "no rows affected" — a fourth distinct 404 shape on this API.
claims.evidence: PUT /wm/picks/resetPicks/batch with a whole pick record from wave SPTEST10 -> 404 {"errorCode":"-1403","userMessage":"no rows affected"}.
observed: The four 404 shapes now are: ROUTE-MISSING ({"message":"Not Found","url":...}), RECORD-MISSING ({timestamp,responseId,errors}), CSRF-REJECTED (empty body), and this one — route and record both fine, but the update matched nothing.
Unlike the other three, this 404 means the request was understood: it is closer to a no-op report than to a routing failure.

claims.claim: POST /wm/orderLines/cancelLines cancels a real order line. The payload is a FIVE-KEY SUBSET — {clientId, orderLine, orderNumber, orderSubLine, warehouseId} — not the whole record.
claims.evidence: Order 2096557293 line 0001: cancelledFlag false -> true, async group CANCEL-ORDER-LINE settled COMPLETE, resultId "----*!0001*!2096557293*!0000*!SG".
observed: Sending the WHOLE order line record first returned a bare 400 "Bad Request" with errorCode null — no hint that the problem was payload width. The five-key shape came from the client bundle (WM.tf.common.documents.OutboundOrder cancelOrderLines), not from the error.
pickQuantity jumped 0 -> 320 as the line was cancelled, so cancelling a line does NOT leave its quantities at rest; a verifier that only checks cancelledFlag misses half the effect.
The resultId is a *!-delimited composite of clientId, orderLine, orderNumber, orderSubLine and warehouseId — the same five keys the payload carries.

claims.claim: POST /wm/orderLines/deleteLines takes a WRAPPER object — {reasonCode, reasonComment, mode:"rmv", orderLines:[…five-key…]} — not an array, and refused a real line with a named business error.
claims.evidence: Order 2096557293 line 0017 -> 200, async group DELETE-ORDER-LINE settled FAILURE errorCode 11869 "Unable to delete order line because it is planned into a shipment." Line count stayed 17.
observed: Route and payload are both confirmed correct — the refusal is a domain rule, not a contract error.
The client also has a pre-flight route, POST /wm/orderLines/validateChange, that takes the SAME wrapper body and reports the failures before anything is deleted.
The wrapper carries an approveCancelPicks flag the UI sets after prompting, for the case where deletion would cancel picks.

claims.claim: POST /wm/crossdocks/cancelCrossDocks removes a cross dock outright, but only when the three flags canflg/remflg/cancod are supplied as QUERY parameters. Without them the same body returns a bare 400.
claims.evidence: XDK0075834 (REPLENISHMENT type, quantity 486, allocated 486): whole record with no query flags -> 400 "Bad Request"; identical body with ?canflg=false&remflg=false&cancod= -> 200 with an empty body, and the cross dock is gone from /wm/crossdocks.
observed: This is the third verb here whose real contract splits across body and query string, after shipments/changeCarrier and locations/massupdate.
Unlike the "cancel" verbs on work and picks — which de-allocate and leave the demand — this one genuinely removes the record.
The 200 carries no body, so the read-back is the only evidence.

claims.claim: PUT /wm/waves/cancelWave/async, sent a bare wave record, settled FAILURE with errorCode 11231 — and the wave changed state regardless, ALOC -> REL.
claims.evidence: Wave SPTEST1: async group CANCELWAVE settled FAILURE, "Cannot deassign all shipment lines that have outstanding picks/replenishments/cross docks." Wave status read back as REL, having been ALOC before the call.
observed: A reported FAILURE is therefore NOT proof that nothing happened. Every prior no-op finding in this project came from the opposite direction (success reported, nothing done); this is the mirror image and is more dangerous, because a failure result invites no verification at all.
Always read the record back after a failed async group, not only after a successful one.
Bare object rather than array, matching unallocateWave — the two wave verbs share a payload convention that differs from every other verb here.

claims.claim: Both documented client paths for cancelling a replenishment fail with 422 errorCode 11630, "An unexpected error has prevented the system from creating the Asynchronous Resource" — the request never becomes an async group at all.
claims.evidence: Target: pending replenishment workRequestNumber 5490663, replenishmentReference RPL2198834, item 0001241000. POST /wm/picking/replenishments/cancelAction/async with the four-key body {workReference, replenishmentReference, orderNumber, orderLine} + ?reallocateFlag=false -> 422/11630. PUT /wm/picking/replenishments/topOff/async with {itemNumber, itemClientId, warehouseId} -> 422/11630. Adding warehouseId "SG" explicitly changed nothing.
observed: The verb-route map had guessed cancelAction for "Cancel Replenishment". The bundle shows the Item screen actually cancels via PUT wm/picking/replenishments/topOff/async keyed by ITEM (itemNumber + itemClientId + warehouseId + cancelCode + errorFlag), while cancelAction is the shorts-grid path keyed by workReference/replenishmentReference/orderNumber/orderLine. The map named the wrong one of two real routes — a failure mode distinct from naming a route that does not exist.

Error 11630 sits in front of the domain layer, so it says nothing about whether the payload was right; it is not the "record missing" or "business refused" answer, it is "the async framework would not even start".
This is the one verb of the fifteen with no confirmed effect and no confirmed refusal.
claims.superseded_note: The 422/11630 was missing site context, not a blocked async layer. With siteId+subsites the same four-key body cancels the replenishment. The observation that the verb map named the wrong one of two real routes still stands.

claims.claim: Three different async URI shapes were observed in one session: the posted path plus /{id}/resources, a batch- infix the request never contained, and a generic /wm/asynch… path shared by unrelated verbs.
claims.evidence: releasePicks -> /wm/picks/releasePicks/batch/async/{id}/resources; confirm -> /wm/picks/confirm/BATCH/async/{id}/resources though it was posted to /wm/picks/confirm/async; cancelLines and deleteLines -> /wm/asynch… .
observed: Any code that builds the polling URI from the request path is wrong for at least two of these three families, and the failure is silent — it polls a URL that does not exist and reports "did not settle".
Only asynchronousResources_uri from the response body is reliable.

claims.claim: PUT /wm/inventory/adjust derives the adjustment from scannedQuantity — the COUNTED quantity — and ignores inventoryAdjustmentQuantity. Sending scannedQuantity 0 against a 55-unit detail queues a -55 adjustment, whatever inventoryAdjustmentQuantity says.
claims.evidence: Two calls with inventoryAdjustmentQuantity +1 and -1, both with scannedQuantity 0, against LPN 00000776442003821453 (unitQuantity 55). Both produced approval rows with adjustmentQuantity -55. See DAMAGE.md §2.
observed: The client payload carries unitQuantity, inventoryAdjustmentQuantity and scannedQuantity together with nothing to say which is authoritative — and the one whose NAME reads as the delta is not the one that counts.
Any "adjust by N" helper written from the field names alone writes off the whole detail instead.

claims.claim: The adjust route has two gates before it does anything: a configured device code, and an approval queue. With no deviceCode it answers 422 errorCode 11309 "Device Code has to be configured before doing this"; with a real one it answers 200 {"approvalRequired": true} and writes a row to /wm/inventoryAdjustmentApprovals rather than changing stock.
claims.evidence: deviceCode absent -> 422/11309. deviceCode "000" (read from /wm/devices) -> 200 with {"approvalRequired":true}; on-hand stayed 55 and two rows appeared in /wm/inventoryAdjustmentApprovals.
observed: The first attempt, missing both a reason code and a device code, returned a bare 500 with errorCode null — no clue which precondition was unmet. Supplying the reason code turned the 500 into the NAMED 11309, so on this API a 500 can simply mean "an unnamed precondition is missing".

approvalRequired: true is the whole response — success here means "queued", not "applied". A verifier that reads on-hand and sees no change would wrongly call this a silent no-op; the effect is real, it is just one step removed.
DELETE /wm/inventoryAdjustmentApprovals/{rowId} returns an empty-bodied 404, so queued rows cannot be withdrawn over this path.

claims.claim: GET /wm/inventory answers 200 with an EMPTY data array on this instance. The inventory rows live on /wm/structuredInventory.
claims.evidence: /wm/inventory?limit=3 -> 200 {"data":[]}; /wm/structuredInventory?limit=3 -> 200 with 3 rows.
observed: A 200 with an empty array is indistinguishable from "this warehouse has no inventory" — the route is not dead, it just is not the one that holds the data.
Consistent with the already-recorded finding that the same concept is keyed differently per resource (label "LPN" is loadNumber on Inventory, lpn on structuredInventory).

claims.claim: 55 of the 57 unproven write routes have their call site readable in the loaded client bundles, so no payload on this API ever has to be guessed.
claims.evidence: index/route-contracts.json (raw excerpts) and index/route-contracts-derived.json (body keys, query keys, enclosing function per route).
observed: The two without a call site are reached only from lazily loaded QuickApp bundles that did not load on the screens visited.

This retires guessing as a method here: three separate failures this project recorded — a -55 write-off, a bare 400 for a too-wide payload, a bare 400 for missing query flags — were all answered by the bundle text, not by the error responses.
Mining is read-only and costs no session time against the API, so it should precede every write attempt from now on.

claims.claim: The work-order family — /wm/workOrders, /wm/workOrderLines — answers 200 with an EMPTY array on this instance. The five work-order write routes cannot be exercised against real records here.
claims.evidence: /wm/workOrders?limit=20 -> 200, 0 rows. /wm/workOrderLines -> 200, 0 rows. /wm/workOrderTypes -> 200 with 2 rows, so the module IS configured, just unused. Only two work-order screens exist in the app map, both configuration screens.
observed: All four mined work-order routes (deallocate, moveWorkOrder, requestFinishedGoods, confirmedWorkOrder) share one contract: {workOrderNumber, clientId, warehouseId, workOrderRevision}, with pickQuantity/pickCatchQuantity added for the two line-level ones.
The contract is therefore known and recorded, but no round trip is possible without first creating a work order — and the mined POST /wm/workOrders is an action on an existing order, not a create.
This is a DATA gap, not an effort gap: no amount of further work closes it on this instance.

claims.claim: Probing seventeen domains separates three distinct states that all look like "no coverage" from the outside: not deployed (404), deployed but empty (200 with zero rows), and populated.
claims.evidence: NOT DEPLOYED: transportEquipment. DEPLOYED BUT EMPTY: workOrders, workOrderLines, noLocationReplens. POPULATED: shipments, shipmentLines (73,068), unassignedShipments, crossdocks, replenishmentConfigurations, workOrderTypes. Collection-level 405: handlingUnits, splitShipments, locationaudit, inventoryStatus. Needs a filter (422): cycleCounts, workAssignments, workflowOperations.
observed: A 405 at the collection means the resource exists but is not listable — those are write-only or sub-resource-only paths, and a coverage sweep that treats 405 as failure will under-report.
A 422 "Maximum rows exceeded" means the resource is real and populated but refuses an unfiltered read — the same shape /wm/picks gives.
Only the populated group can ever yield a round trip. Sizing remaining work by counting routes, rather than by which have data behind them, overstates what is achievable.

claims.claim: Error 11630, "An unexpected error has prevented the system from creating the Asynchronous Resource", is a GENERIC async-group-creation failure. Missing site context is one cause — supplying siteId fixed it on cancelledShipmentLines — but it is not the meaning of the error.
claims.evidence: PUT /wm/shipmentLines/cancelledShipmentLines with body [{shipmentLineId:"SLN000436H"}]: bare path -> 422/11630; ?siteId=SG&subsites=---- -> 200 with group CANCEL-SHIPMENT-LINE; ?siteId=SG&warehouseId=SG -> 200 likewise. Same body throughout.
observed: The message is actively misleading — it reads as a server fault and names nothing the caller controls. Two verbs (Cancel Replenishment, Cancel Shipment Line) were recorded as unresolvable on the strength of it.

The requirement is NOT universal: /wm/waves/cancelWave/async created its group with no site params at all. So 11630 is a per-route requirement, and the only reliable move is to send the site context on every async write.

Isolated by varying one thing at a time against a line the UI itself would have allowed cancelling (shipment status R, pickedQuantity 0). Widening the body instead — adding shipmentId, sending the whole record, sending a bare object — produced bare 400s, i.e. every wrong guess about the BODY looks different from this.
CORRECTION 2026-08-19: generalising from the one case where site context fixed it was wrong. Two routes now return 11630 for reasons that are not site context at all.
claims.correction: Originally recorded as "11630 means missing site context". locationList/async then returned 11630 with siteId present, with subsites single, with subsites repeated exactly as the client sends it, and with siteId alone — and also when the CLIENT'S OWN model save issued it. So 11630 says only that the async layer would not build the group; the caller must diagnose why case by case.

claims.claim: PUT /wm/shipmentLines/cancelledShipmentLines cancels a real shipment line: lineStatus P (Pending) -> B (Canceled).
claims.evidence: Shipment SID0009108 line SLN000436H, read back from /wm/shipments/SID0009108/shipmentLines: "Pending" before, "Canceled" after. Async group type CANCEL-SHIPMENT-LINE.
observed: Body is an array of {shipmentLineId} only — adding shipmentId, or sending the whole record, returns a bare 400.

The bundle reads b.get("shipmentLine") but both /wm/shipmentLines and the shipment sub-resource expose the value as shipmentLineId; here the two names carry the SAME value, unlike other divergences recorded in this project.
The client gates this action on shipment status READY/INPROCESS/LOADING and pickedQuantity === 0 — worth honouring, since the server accepted a line the UI would also have allowed.

claims.claim: POST /wm/picking/replenishments/cancelAction/async cancels a real replenishment outright once the site context is supplied. The replenishment disappears from pendingReplenishments.
claims.evidence: Replenishment workRequestNumber 5490663 / RPL2198834 (item 0001241000, wave SPTEST3): 200 with async group REPLENISHMENT, settled COMPLETE errorCode null, resultId "SPTEST3|0001". Read back: gone.
observed: Body is an array of {workReference, replenishmentReference, orderNumber, orderLine}; reallocateFlag rides in the query string alongside siteId/subsites.
This supersedes the earlier FALSIFIED claim cancel-replenishment-blocked-at-the-async-layer — the payload was right all along; only the site context was missing.
Note orderNumber on a replenishment carries the WAVE number (SPTEST3), not an order number.

claims.claim: PUT /wm/picks/resetPicks/batch reaches the domain layer and correctly reports that no row qualifies: every pick on this instance is already released (pickStatus R) with appliedQuantity 0, which is the state a reset would produce.
claims.evidence: With site context supplied: whole pick record -> 404 errorCode -1403 "no rows affected"; bare {workRequestId} -> 200 with an empty body. Neither moved workRequestId 5490678 (pickStatus R, PEND, applied 0).
observed: The two payload shapes give DIFFERENT answers to the same non-qualifying request — one a 404 that names the situation, one a silent 200. The 404 is the more honest of the two.
This is a data gap, not a contract gap: resetting requires a pick with work applied to it, and none exists here.
claims.overturned_note: Wrong. The census behind it came from /wm/waves/{n}/picks (all status R). consolidatedPicks — the resource the actions bind — held a pick in status E, and Reset moved it E -> P. The route was never the problem; the sample was.

claims.claim: POST /wm/shipments/cancelledShipments cancels a whole shipment: shipmentStatus R (Ready) -> B (Cancelled). It answers synchronously with the full updated shipment record, not with an async group.
claims.evidence: Shipment SID0019363: 200, body is the whole shipment; read back as status B "Cancelled".
observed: Body is a BARE object {shipmentId}; the query carries preventRecursionMode plus the site context.

preventRecursionMode is an ENUM, not a boolean — the bundle sends "DIRECT". Sending "false" returns 422 errorCode 810 "Invalid argument: prcmod", which names the SERVER-SIDE parameter (prcmod), not the one the client sent. That mapping is invisible from the client side and the error is the only place it surfaces.
Unlike the other cancel verbs in this family, this one is synchronous — no async group to poll.

claims.claim: POST /wm/shipments/shipmentPlan reaches the domain layer and refuses with a named error when the order line already belongs to a load: 422 errorCode 11900.
claims.evidence: Order 2096557293 line 0002 -> 422, "Assignment not allowed. Order line [2096557293] - [----] - [SG] - [0002] - [0000] is already assigned to a load."
observed: Route and payload (an array of {orderNumber, orderLine, orderSubLine, warehouseId, clientId}) are confirmed correct — the refusal is a domain rule.
The error echoes the full composite key, which is the clearest identifier echo seen from this API.
Proving the success path needs an order line not yet on a load; every line on the test order is assigned.

claims.claim: POST /wm/shipments/ is not an action. It is the Ext model's own create/proxy URL, picked up by route mining because the client builds it with the same buildDataServiceUrl call as real verbs.
claims.evidence: Posting with shipmentId in the query (the shape the derived contract suggested) returns a bare 400 on both a live and a cancelled shipment. The nearby function triggerShipmentStageWorkflow actually builds a WORKFLOW_CRITERIA object and posts to the workflowOperations routes, not to /wm/shipments/.
observed: Route mining finds every URL the bundle constructs, including model proxy URLs and tooltip reads — a mined route is a CANDIDATE, not evidence that a verb exists.

The derived contract attributed the nearest enclosing function name to the route, and here that pairing was wrong. Where the derived body/query keys come from a different function than the route, the raw excerpt has to be read.
This is the counterweight to the 70-write-route figure: some fraction of it is proxy noise, so "routes with no proven exchange" overstates the real remaining work.

claims.claim: Five of the open routes are compute-or-validate utilities, and all five answer correctly with real inputs: wm/sequences, wm/commands/generateNextNumber, wm/serverStatus, wm/pickEstimates/shipments, wm/orderLines/validateChange.
claims.evidence: sequences {numCod:"sesnum",qty:1} -> [{"nxtNum":"SES0088083"}]. generateNextNumber GET ?numcod=sesnum -> [{"nxtnum":"SES0088084"}]. serverStatus {mocaServiceUrl:"…"} -> {mocaServiceUrl,online:false}. pickEstimates {wh_id:"SG",shipNumList:"SID0009108"} -> estimates (casePicks 20, estimatedPallets 8, estimatedWeight 66506.88). validateChange with the deleteLines wrapper -> async group VALIDATE-CHANGE-ORDER-LINE.
observed: For these, a successful response IS the proof — they compute rather than mutate, so there is no record to read back. That is a distinct proof class from every write recorded so far.

The SAME concept appears under two key spellings on one route pair: sequences takes numCod while generateNextNumber takes numcod, and they return nxtNum and nxtnum respectively. Case is significant on both.

generateNextNumber is a model PROXY, so it answers to GET, not the PUT the route mining implied. A method mined from a bundle is the method of whatever call site was nearest, not necessarily the route's own.
pickEstimates takes RAW DB KEYS — wh_id and shipNumList — where every neighbouring route takes camelCase. Sending warehouseId/shipmentId returns a bare 400.

claims.claim: PUT /wm/locationaudit/validatelocations reports 422 errorCode 802 "Missing argument: Warehouse ID (wh_id)" no matter where wh_id is supplied — query string, inside each body record, or both, with and without subsites.
claims.evidence: Seven variants tried: array vs JSON-stringified array body (the bundle stringifies it); wh_id / whId / warehouseId in the query; wh_id inside each record; all three spellings at once; with and without subsites. Every array-bodied variant -> 422/802; every stringified variant -> bare 400.
observed: The two body shapes fail DIFFERENTLY — a stringified body never reaches the argument check, so the 400 and the 422 are at different layers. The array body is the one getting through.
The records were read from /wm/locations, but the client feeds this route from its own LocationAudit grid model, which likely carries fields a plain location row does not.
Resolution path is a UI capture, the same method that cracked locations/massupdate: drive the Location Audit screen and record what it actually sends. Black-box variation has been exhausted.

claims.claim: PUT /wm/inventoryStatus/async changes a real inventory detail's status and back: AV (AVAILABLE) -> AG (AGE HOLD) -> AV.
claims.evidence: Detail D00000056ORS on LPN 00000776442003821453: both directions 200 with async group INVENTORYSTATUS, settled COMPLETE errorCode null, verified by re-reading /wm/structuredInventory.
observed: Body is an array of {toInventoryStatus, warehouseId, mode:"GUI", reasonCode, detailNumber}. The client picks detailNumber / subNumber / loadNumber according to the record's inventoryLevel — detail is the narrowest and the one used here.
reasonCode was null and the call still succeeded, so the reason code is optional on this route (unlike inventory/adjust, where its absence turned a named error into a bare 500).
resultId came back as "SG" — the SITE, not the record. Several routes echo a useful composite id; this one does not, so the read-back is the only way to attribute the effect.
There is no readable status vocabulary: /wm/inventoryStatuses 404s and /wm/inventoryStatus is write-only. The valid codes had to be sampled from real inventory rows — AV (194 of 200), AG (5), DE (1).

claims.claim: POST /wm/inventory/changeInvAttribute reaches the domain layer and refuses: 422 errorCode 11520, "Cannot change inv_attr for inventory whose item is not inv_attr tracked". No item on this instance is attribute-tracked.
claims.evidence: Detail D00000056ORS, field inventoryAttributeText1 -> 422/11520. Across 200 inventory rows, zero carry any inventoryAttribute* value; across 200 items there is no attribute-tracking flag at all (only lotTrackingFlag, true everywhere).
observed: The body is an array of {field, value} pairs — the same shape as locations/massupdate — but the SELECTION travels inside that array too, as the pseudo-fields wh_id and dtlnum_list, rather than as a query filter. Two mass-update routes, two different places to put the selection.
Contract confirmed by the named refusal; proving the effect needs UDIA (user-defined inventory attributes) enabled on an item, which this instance does not have.

claims.claim: POST /wm/inventory/move/async moves a real LPN between locations, and back: RB327A -> RA118A -> RB327A.
claims.evidence: LPN 00000776442003821453 (55 units), async group PUTAWAY, both moves settled COMPLETE, each verified by re-reading /wm/structuredInventory.
observed: destinationLoadNumber must be NULL for a plain location move. Naming the source LPN there — which reads as the natural thing to do — fails with 10586 "Invalid destination location (Current LPN already exists)", because the route treats that field as the LPN to move inventory INTO.
The destination must be a peer slot. Both "000" (a dummy) and the numeric SPEXPR order-bound slots fail 10586; an empty location in the SAME areaCode as the source works.
The async group is typed PUTAWAY, not MOVE — the group type does not always name the verb that created it.
resultId is null on success and the LPN only on failure, so success carries less identifying information than failure does.

claims.claim: A revert that reuses the identifiers captured BEFORE the write can fail against the record it just changed: reverting the LPN move with the original sourceLocation returned 10259 "Bad source location", because the LPN was no longer there.
claims.evidence: Move RB327A -> RA118A settled COMPLETE. The revert call still named sourceLocation RB327A and failed 10259, leaving the LPN in RA118A until a second pass re-read its position and moved it home.
observed: For field updates a stale before-image is harmless — the identifier does not change. For MOVES the identifier IS the thing that changed, so the before-image is invalid the moment the write succeeds.
Any restore step must re-read the record and move from wherever it actually is, not from where it was.
This is why every write here is paired with a verifying read: the failed revert was visible immediately rather than being discovered later as unexplained drift.

claims.claim: Both general work-save routes work on a real work record: PUT /wm/work/batch (synchronous) and PUT /wm/work/async (async group) each set effectivePriority and set it back.
claims.evidence: Work 5490416 (PEND): via /wm/work/batch 2 -> 9 -> 2, each call 200 returning the updated records. Via /wm/work/async 2 -> 8 -> 2, 202 with an async group settling COMPLETE, resultId "5490416".
observed: Body for both is an array of WHOLE work records with the field changed — the same convention as the wave-priority write.
work/batch answers synchronously with the updated rows; work/async returns a group to poll. Two routes, same resource, same payload, different response models — the caller has to know which is which.

claims.claim: manualWorkSequence cannot be set on a PEND work row: PUT /wm/work/async settles FAILURE with errorCode -1403 "no rows affected", while the SAME route and record accept a change to effectivePriority.
claims.evidence: Work 5490416: manualWorkSequence null -> 77 settled FAILURE -1403, still null. Immediately afterwards effectivePriority 2 -> 8 on the same route settled COMPLETE and read back as 8.
observed: The control is what makes this readable. Without it, -1403 looks like "this route does not work"; with it, the route is proven and the FIELD is the constraint.
Worth generalising: when a whole-record write reports no rows affected, retry the same route with a field already known to be settable before concluding anything about the route.
Zero of 200 work rows carry a manualWorkSequence, consistent with the field being set only in states this instance does not hold.

claims.claim: releaseHeldPicks, resetUnassignedPicks and workAssignments/removePicks are each gated on a pick state that does not exist here — every pick on this instance is pickStatus R.
claims.evidence: Wave SPTEST10 picks are 29/29 pickStatus R. releaseHeldPicks (client gate: all picks H) -> 200 empty body, no change. resetUnassignedPicks -> 200 empty body, no change. removePicks (client gate: all picks E) -> 202, async group REMOVEPICK, settled FAILURE -1403 "no rows affected". Pick unchanged after all three.
observed: The two synchronous ones answer 200 with an EMPTY body and no error when their gate is unmet; the async one at least reports -1403. Same class of non-event, three different signatures.

The client refuses to call these at all unless every selected pick matches (it alerts instead), so the server-side non-answer is normally never seen — an agent calling the API directly WILL see it and must not read it as success.
For removePicks the client first copies workTask into workReference; that was reproduced here.

CORRECTION 2026-08-19: the pick census behind this claim came from /wm/waves/{n}/picks, which is NOT the resource the pick actions bind. The Picks screen store reads wm/picks/consolidatedPicks (244 fields per row). Measured there, the distribution is R 183, E 1, C 16 — not "R only". The conclusion that no HELD pick exists still holds, but it was reached from the wrong resource, which is the same class of error that made validatelocations look unusable.

claims.claim: PUT /wm/replenishmentConfigurations/{resourceId} edits a real replenishment configuration and back: incrementUnits 100 -> 150 -> 100.
claims.evidence: Config RCF0000CZN (item 0001072000): both calls 200 returning the updated record, verified by re-reading the collection.
observed: This route is an ordinary rpRest model proxy, so it follows the plain record-PUT convention — send the whole record with the field changed, minus the server-owned *_uri fields.
It appeared in the mined write list looking like an action route; it is simply CRUD on a config resource.

claims.claim: rolePickDeductions, orderTypePickDeductions and pickZonePickDeductions all return 200 with zero rows, so their /sequences sub-resource writes have no parent to attach to.
claims.evidence: All three collections -> 200, n=0. The client posts an array of sequence objects either to a parent's sequences_uri or to the collection route; with no parent record, neither is reachable.
observed: These are sub-resource writes, so their testability depends entirely on parent data — a distinct kind of no-data from "the domain is empty".
Creating a parent was not attempted: the parent create is not among the mined routes, so it would have meant guessing a contract, which this project has already paid for twice.

claims.claim: POST /wm/unassignedShipments/assignShipments puts a real shipment on a load, and POST /wm/commands/cancelWorkUnassignShipmentFromStop takes it off again.
claims.evidence: Shipment SID0009108 onto load LD00003073: async group ASSIGN-SHIPMENT settled COMPLETE, resultId "SID0009108", carrierMoveId read back as LD00003073. Unassign -> 200 with [{"successful":1}], carrierMoveId back to null.
observed: assignShipments takes an array of WHOLE shipment records with carrierMoveId set to the target load.

The unassign route was not in the open list — it was found by grepping the mined routes for "unassign" before making the change, so the reversal was known before the write. Worth doing routinely for anything without an obvious undo.
Its body is [{ship_id}] — the raw DB key again, a third instance after pickEstimates (wh_id, shipNumList) and locationaudit (wh_id).

claims.claim: PUT /wm/picking/replenishments/topOff/async is the CANCEL path for top-off replenishments, and says so: 11962 "There are no active topoff replenishments to cancel."
claims.evidence: Item 0001072000 / client ----: 200, async group REPLENISHMENT, settled FAILURE 11962, resultId "0001072000*!----".
observed: The error message confirms the reading taken from the bundle: the Item screen's "Cancel Replenishment" posts here, keyed by item, while the shorts grid uses cancelAction keyed by reference.
Contract confirmed by a named refusal. No active top-off replenishments exist here, so the effect cannot be shown.

claims.claim: POST /wm/outboundOrders/changeCarrier builds its async group correctly and then settles FAILURE with errorCode 502 "Unexpected server error" for every carrier code tried.
claims.evidence: Order 000031626918: carrier codes 001, SONOCO and RBLT each -> 200, async group CHANGE-CARRIER, settled FAILURE 502, resultId "----*!000031626918*!SG" (the correct composite key).
observed: The derived contract was WRONG here: car_move_id/new_carcod belonged to a neighbouring call site. The real order-level contract is a body of {clientId, outboundOrderNumber, warehouseId} with carrierCode and serviceLevel as query params — and with that, the request is accepted and the resultId names the right order.
Pairs with the earlier finding that shipments/changeCarrier silently no-ops. Two routes, two failure modes, same verb: changing a carrier does not work on this instance by either path.
The outboundOrders resource exposes no plain carrier field (only carrierDetails_uri and a changeCarrier flag), so even a successful change would need the sub-resource to verify.

claims.claim: POST /wm/inventory/massupdate selects rows from the {field,value} list itself, and refuses with 422 errorCode 540 "Maximum rows exceeded in query" when that selection is too broad — even though a dtlnum_list naming one detail was supplied.
claims.evidence: Client ownership transfer of detail D00000056ORS (item 0113228000) from ---- to NEWTEST19 -> 422/540. itemClientId unchanged.
observed: This is the good outcome: the route REFUSED rather than transferring ownership of every detail of that item. A mass-update endpoint whose scope is expressed as ordinary-looking fields is one wrong key away from a warehouse-wide write.
dtlnum_list did not narrow it the way it does on changeInvAttribute, so the two field-list routes scope differently despite sharing a payload shape.
Do not retry this by widening the field list until the real UI request has been captured — the failure mode of a wrong guess here is not an error, it is a bulk change.

claims.claim: Four entries in the mined write list are PATH PREFIXES that the client completes with a record id or an action name before calling: wm/shipments/, wm/waves/, wm/inventory/ and wm/handlingUnits/.
claims.evidence: wm/waves/ is built as wm/waves/{resourceId}/{action} (removeFromWaveWebService). wm/inventory/ appears as wm/inventory/{id}/validateInventoryIdentifier. wm/handlingUnits/ is completed with emptyReceivingHandlingUnit or emptyShipmentHandlingUnit. wm/shipments/ is the Ext model proxy URL. Each returns a bare 400 when called as-is.
observed: Route mining captures the literal handed to buildDataServiceUrl(), which for these is only the stem — the trailing id or verb is concatenated at the call site.
A trailing slash in the mined path is the tell: all four end in "/", and none of the confirmed real verbs do.
This matters for sizing: the raw write-route count includes prefixes and model proxies, so it overstates the number of actual verbs. Of 70 mined write routes, 5 are now classified not-a-verb.

claims.claim: POST /wm/cycleCounts/async generates a cycle count on a real location and PUT on the same route cancels it — same path, same body, the METHOD is the verb.
claims.evidence: Location RB327A, body [{storageLocation, warehouseId, requestCountBy:"PART_LOC"}]. Generate -> countHistory gained CH00008ESO and countInProgressDetails gained a row with countStatus R. Cancel -> countInProgressDetails empty. Both settled COMPLETE with resultId "1".
observed: The parent location's own countInProgress flag stayed FALSE the whole time, and numberOfCounts stayed 0, while its countInProgressDetails sub-resource clearly held a running count. The parent's summary fields do not reflect its own children — verifying against the parent would have reported a silent no-op for a write that plainly worked.
resultId is "1" — a count of affected rows, not an identifier. Another response field that looks like an id and is not.

claims.claim: POST /explainSqlQuery returns a real query plan, and PUT /wm/devices/{id} updates a device record — the 405 seen earlier was the COLLECTION refusing, not the route.
claims.evidence: explainSqlQuery?sql=select 1 from dual -> 200 with a plan row (type SELECT, totalsubtreecost 1.157e-6). PUT /wm/devices/000*!SG with the record unchanged -> 200 returning the record.
observed: A 405 at a collection says nothing about the record-level route. Three routes in this sweep (devices, handlingUnits, splitShipments) answer 405 at the collection while being perfectly real one level down.
explainSqlQuery is a query planner exposed straight through the data service — read-shaped and safe, but worth flagging as an unusual surface to have available.

claims.claim: POST /reporting/reports/reportBookmark creates a bookmark (201) and PUT updates it (200), but DELETE on the same path returns 405 — there is no API route to remove one.
claims.evidence: Created RPTBMRK-20260819084827_755006 on report BP-PackingList, updated its bookmarkDetails, then DELETE -> 405 Method Not Allowed. The unnested path /reporting/reportBookmark 404s; only the nested one under /reports/ exists.
observed: The created id comes back NESTED as data.reportBookmark.bookmarkId, not at the top level — an id-extraction that assumes the usual shape misses it.
DELETE /reporting/reports/{id} with an impossible id returns 200, so that route gives no record-missing signal at all: a delete of something that never existed is indistinguishable from a real one.

claims.claim: The Location Audit grid has no read proxy — loading it throws "c.proxy.read is not a function". It is populated by audit RESULTS, so the audit input comes from the filter combo, not from the grid.
claims.evidence: Store load on locationauditGrid -> TypeError from ext-all. The Start Audit button is enabled but sends nothing while the grid is empty.
observed: This is why validatelocations could not be captured by clicking: there was nothing selected to audit. The next attempt must drive the rpFilterComboBox to select locations first.
It also explains the 802 wh_id failures indirectly — the controller derives its request from the filter context, which a hand-built body does not carry.
Recorded as the concrete next step rather than another round of payload guessing.

claims.claim: The client sends subsites as a REPEATED query parameter — subsites=----&subsites=NEWTEST19&subsites=RUDRAKSH&subsites=TESTSRO&subsites=TRYNEWSRO9 — one value per client.
claims.evidence: Observed off the wire on rpux/persistence/ while the Location Audit screen loaded.
observed: This is the mechanism behind "Argument [warehouseId] has an unexpected number of values" on sub-resources: subsites expands to one value per client, and a sub-resource that already scopes itself by its parent then sees several.
It also means subsites=---- alone, which this project has sent on every call, is NOT what the client sends — it is a single-client abbreviation of a multi-value parameter.

claims.claim: Issuing a call through the page's own RP.Ajax.request reproduces everything the real UI supplies — siteId, the repeated per-client subsites list, the CSRF header, the referer — without having to drive the screen. It settles "is this a payload problem?" in one call.
claims.evidence: Driving the Location Audit screen failed for structural reasons (its grid is an output store; components move between two same-URL frames; stores reset between passes). RP.Ajax with the controller's own request object reproduced the exact wire form: PUT wm/locationaudit/validatelocations?siteId=SG&subsites=----&subsites=NEWTEST19&subsites=RUDRAKSH&subsites=TESTSRO&subsites=TRYNEWSRO9 with the whole location record as body.
observed: This changes the method for every remaining blocked route: rather than reverse-engineering a screen, hand the mined request object to the client's own transport and read the answer.

It also immediately found a REAL difference: workflowOperations/initiation returns 400 to a raw fetch sending a JSON-encoded STRING, and 200 to RP.Ajax sending an object. The bundle line Ext.JSON.encode(b) misled me — Ext re-encodes, so passing an already-encoded string double-encodes it.

claims.claim: PUT /wm/locationaudit/validatelocations answers 422 errorCode 802 "Missing argument: Warehouse ID (wh_id)" even when called through the client's own transport with the controller's own request object. The payload was never the problem.
claims.evidence: Via RP.Ajax with the whole location record and the client's own URL: 422/802. Then with params wh_id, whId, warehouseId, and wh_id plus repairMode/noLockMode: 422/802 in every case. Earlier: seven raw-fetch variants, same error.
observed: The client would fail identically. This is not a contract gap that a UI capture could close — the argument is expected to arrive from the service layer and does not on this deployment.
Eleven distinct attempts across two transports now agree, which is as close to settled as a black-box result gets.
wm/locationaudit/repairlocations/async is the same family and the same blocker.
claims.overturned_note: Wrong conclusion. Eleven attempts across two transports all sent /wm/locations rows, whose keys are warehouseId and storageLocation. The audit loads from wm/locationaudit/locationforaudit, whose model uses "warehouse" and "location". With those names the route answers 200. The evidence was consistent because every attempt shared the same mistake — agreement across attempts is not independence.

claims.claim: POST /wm/workflowOperations/initiation succeeds through the client transport (200, data []). POST /wm/inventory/stockTransfer/async builds its async group and then fails in allocation: errorCode 12035.
claims.evidence: initiation with {exitPoint:"SHIPSTG", warehouseId:"SG"} -> 200 {"data":[]}. stockTransfer -> group 1566098, runner StockMoveInventoryTrackedRunnerImpl, FAILURE 12035 "An unexpected error occurred during allocation". workflowOperations/reverse -> 500.
observed: The empty data array from initiation means no workflow matched that exit point — the route works, the criteria found nothing. Real criteria keys live in WM.util.Constants.WORKFLOW_CRITERIA.
The async resource names its own Java runner class, which is the most specific implementation detail this API has surfaced anywhere — useful for correlating a failure with server logs.

claims.claim: POST /wm/inventory/massupdate with an impossible dtlnum_list but a real itemNumber does not return within 25 seconds. Nothing was changed, but the call does not fail fast either.
claims.evidence: Scope probe via RP.Ajax timed out at 25s. Verification afterwards: all 200 inventory rows still on client ----, item 0113228000 still single-client, detail D00000056ORS unchanged (qty 55, RB327A, AV).
observed: Combined with the earlier 540 "Maximum rows exceeded", the picture is that this route scopes on the ITEM and scans, rather than honouring dtlnum_list the way changeInvAttribute does.
The probe was deliberately given an impossible detail so that a wrong scope would be visible as a refusal rather than as a bulk write. It was — and the verification pass confirmed nothing moved.
Left BLOCKED on purpose. A route that scans on a real item and hangs is not one to explore by widening the payload.

claims.claim: DELETE works on both /mcs/mediaLinks and /reporting/reports — proven by creating a record of my own and removing that, rather than deleting shared config.
claims.evidence: Media link: POST against an existing mediaId (MED00000000000102) with my own associationKey -> 201; DELETE /mcs/mediaLinks/{resourceId} -> 200; link absent on re-read, 96 links before and after. Report: POST reportId ZZAUDIT-TEST -> 201; DELETE -> 200; direct GET afterwards -> 404.
observed: The create is what made the delete testable. POST /mcs/mediaLinks with an invented mediaId is refused with a NAMED error — 2003 "Invalid value (Media ID: ZZAUDIT) for Media" — so reusing a real media id with a fresh association key was the way in.

The report create returns 201 with an EMPTY body, and the new report did not appear in a limit=50 listing because the id sorts last; a limit=200 read found it among 87. A create that returns nothing plus a paged listing is an easy way to believe a write failed when it worked.
resourceId for a media link is a composite of the association key and media id joined by *!, and the association key is itself an XML fragment — it must be URL-encoded whole for the DELETE path.

claims.claim: The workflow criteria key is "exitpoint" (lowercase p) with "exitpointType", read from WM.util.Constants.WORKFLOW_CRITERIA — not the camelCase exitPoint a reader would assume.
claims.evidence: Constants read live from the page. WORKFLOW_CRITERIA.COMMON = {WAREHOUSEID:"warehouseId", EXITPOINT:"exitpoint", EXITPOINT_TYPE:"exitpointType", PICK_CONFIRM:"pickConfirm"}. EXITPOINTS enumerates ~40 codes across INBOUND/OUTBOUND (SHIPSTG, OUTBOUND-SHIP, POST-PICK, LOADTRLR, …).
observed: Note the inconsistency inside one constants block: warehouseId is camelCase while exitpoint is not.
Initiation answers 200 with data [] for every exit point and every configured workflow name tried, so the lookup runs but matches nothing without the full record context the real caller supplies.
The twelve configured workflows are named INIT-SAFETY-CHECK, USR-CHEP-CHCK, SET-OPTIMAL-STG-LANE, UC-AMZN-AUTO-CLOSE and similar — all site-specific customisations, keyed SG*!<name>.

claims.claim: POST /wm/locationList/async returns 422/11630 even when the request is issued by the client's own LocationRange model via save(), which serialises exactly what the proxy expects.
claims.evidence: Ext model save produced POST wm/locationList/async?siteId=SG&subsites=----&subsites=NEWTEST19&subsites=RUDRAKSH&subsites=TESTSRO&subsites=TRYNEWSRO9 with body {"conflicts":"","endRange":"ZZAUDIT01","locationCount":1,"startRange":"ZZAUDIT01"} -> 422. The same body by hand, with single / repeated / siteId-only query forms -> 422/11630 in every case. No ZZAUDIT01 location was created.
observed: The body is a BARE OBJECT, not an array — mining had suggested an array, and the model settled it.
Same conclusion as validatelocations: the client itself cannot call this successfully here, so it is not a contract gap that further work could close.
Using the client MODEL (rec.save()) rather than raw transport is the strongest form of this test — it removes serialisation from the list of suspects entirely.

FOLLOW-UP: the location generator does not use this route at all. It uses the MOCA commands generateLocationList, createLocationList and removeLocation. wm/locationList/async is the create URL of a model the generator screen does not drive — vestigial, which is why nothing can make it work.

claims.claim: No shipment on this instance has staged inventory: all eight read return an empty structuredInventory sub-resource, so splitShipments/moveLPNs has no LPN to move.
claims.evidence: SID0009108, SID0019363, SID0023275, SID0023427, SID0023446, SID0024940, SID0025757, SID0033861 — each structuredInventory_uri returns 200 with zero rows.
observed: The contract is known from the bundle ({shipId, newShipId, location, newCarrierMoveId, existingCarrierMoveId, shipLineId, lpn, cartonFlag, lpnLevel}) and a sibling route moveShipments/async was found alongside it.
A data gap, not a contract gap — splitting requires picked and staged inventory, and this instance has none against any shipment.

claims.claim: POST /wm/outboundOrders/changeCarrier completes successfully when given a carrier from the order's OWN carrierDetails sub-resource. The earlier 502s came from sending carriers that are not legal for that order.
claims.evidence: Order 000031626918: carrierDetails lists exactly one legal carrier, SONOCO. Sent with its serviceLevel -> async group CHANGE-CARRIER 1566099, runner OutboundOrderActionTrackedRunnerImpl, settled COMPLETE with errorCode null and resultId "----*!000031626918*!SG".
observed: This retires the earlier "blocked, server error" reading. A 502 from this route means the carrier is not valid for the order, not that the route is broken — the validity list is per-order and readable from carrierDetails_uri.

The effect cannot be demonstrated on this instance: all 25 orders checked offer exactly ONE legal carrier, so the verb can only ever be called with the carrier the order already has. Contract proven, state change unobservable.
A general lesson for enumerated arguments: ask the record what it allows before treating a rejection as a server fault.

claims.claim: POST /wm/locations/asyncError and POST /wm/locations/asyncReset are inverses: they move a location between Empty and Inventory Error. Body for both is an array of {warehouseId, storageLocation}.
claims.evidence: Location RA118A: locationStatus E "Empty" -> asyncError -> I "Inventory Error" -> asyncReset -> E "Empty". Both 200 with async group type LOCATION.
observed: These are the Inventory Display screen's "Error Locations" and "Reset Locations" actions.

Neither had a call site in any bundle loaded by visiting screens — they were found by reading the FILE ATTRIBUTION already stored in index/bundle-routes.json, which named WM.tf.inventorydisplay.InventoryDisplay, and fetching that bundle directly. Attribution recorded at mining time paid off much later.
Deriving QuickApp bundle names from class names failed for all 16 candidates tried (404 each) — internal capitalisation cannot be reconstructed. The stored attribution is the reliable route.

claims.claim: The selection for /wm/inventory/massupdate travels as a pseudo-field named "query" whose value is a JSON STRING of [{OR:[{AND:[{column,operator,value,options:{exact:[true]}}, …]}]}] built from loadNumber, subNumber and detailNumber — not dtlnum_list, which is what changeInvAttribute uses.
claims.evidence: Read from getUpdateFieldValues + getMainGridSelection in WM.Common. With that query present the route reaches the domain layer and returns a NAMED refusal — 10239 "Invalid footprint code" — instead of hanging. Without it, an earlier attempt hung past 25s because it matched on itemNumber alone.
observed: This explains the hang exactly: the route was scanning the whole item, not scoping to a detail. Two mass-update routes on the same resource family scope through completely different pseudo-fields.
The refusal is genuine and unfixable here: footprints are client-scoped, and all 13,069 on this instance belong to client ----, so a transfer to NEWTEST19 can never present a valid footprint.
The async URI came back as /wm/inventory/inventory/async/{id}/resources — a DOUBLED path segment, and a fifth distinct async URI shape.

claims.claim: PUT /wm/locationaudit/validatelocations works. The body is an array of records in the AUDIT model's vocabulary — {warehouse, location, noLockMode, repairMode} — not the /wm/locations vocabulary (warehouseId, storageLocation) that every earlier attempt used.
claims.evidence: [{warehouse:"SG", location:"RB327A", noLockMode:true, repairMode:false}] -> 200 with []. Same for an empty location, for two at once, and for a nonexistent code. Previously: 422/802 "Missing argument: Warehouse ID (wh_id)" on every one of eleven attempts.

claims.claim: The pick action routes are fed by wm/picks/consolidatedPicks — the store the Picks screen binds — not by /wm/waves/{waveNumber}/picks. The two resources disagree about what states exist.
claims.evidence: Wave SPTEST10 picks: 29/29 pickStatus R. consolidatedPicks (200 rows): R 183, E 1, C 16. The consolidated row carries 244 fields including workTask, assignedTo and assignedToRole, which the wave sub-resource does not expose.

claims.claim: PUT /wm/workAssignments/removePicks/batch/async returns async FAILURE -1403 "no rows affected" for both the one pick in status E and the one pick that carries an assignment.

observed: The first -1403 was explained by assignedTo being null — the route removes an ASSIGNMENT — but the assigned pick failed identically, so that is not the whole gate either.

The route's own resource, /wm/workAssignments, cannot be read: the standard JSON column filter returns "Syntax error … Expected: <WORD>", and SQL-ish strings return "Could not parse filter query string". Its query dialect is neither, and is not documented anywhere in the client code read so far.
Recorded as unresolved rather than no-data: this instance may well hold a qualifying record that cannot be found without being able to read the assignments resource.

claims.claim: Reset Picks moves a pick from E (error) to P (pending); Release Picks then moves it from P to R (released). Both act on real records and both were previously recorded as having no effect.
claims.evidence: Pick workRequestId 5490618, workTask W0000011IPJR, schedule batch SBDTEST1, order 2094733108, quantity 26. PUT /wm/picks/resetPicks/batch -> 200, pickStatus E -> P. PUT /wm/picks/releasePicks/batch/async -> 202, async COMPLETE, resultId "SBDTEST1|W0000011IPJR|2094733108|26|R", pickStatus P -> R.
observed: Both earlier verdicts failed for the same reason: the pick sampled was already in the state the verb produces. Reset was tried on R (which is post-reset) and Release on R (which is post-release).

The resultId encodes batch | workTask | order | quantity | resulting status — the most informative resultId seen on this API, and it names the END state, which is how the effect can be confirmed from the response alone.
The whole consolidatedPicks record is the payload for both.

claims.claim: The Reset / Reset-Unassigned attempts against a COMPLETED (C) pick cannot be judged: C picks carry workRequestId null, so the before/after matcher keyed on workRequestId compared different rows.

observed: A null identity field silently turns a find() into "first row that also has null there". The comparison looked like a state change and was actually a different record.

Recorded as inconclusive rather than folded into either verdict — the calls happened, the readings are not trustworthy.
